summary:
Tasmania is an Australian state and stands under the national framework carried by the parent record. Within Tasmania, the Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity, gender expression, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics. A September 2013 amendment extended the Act's reach to transgender and intersex people and made it unlawful to offend, humiliate, intimidate, insult or ridicule a person on the basis of actual or perceived gender, sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2019 amendments to the same Act added gender expression, an express definition of gender identity covering being transgender or transsexual and identifying or living as another gender, and sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics, including as grounds for the prohibition on incitement of hatred.

Gender registration on a Tasmanian-registered birth is self-declared. Act 2019 No. 7, amending the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1999, received royal assent on 8 May 2019 and took effect on 5 September 2019: no medical certificate or other medical document is required, and a person aged 16 or over may register male, female, indeterminate gender, non-binary or another self-described gender without parental approval. Parents or guardians may register a gender for a child under 16, supported by the child's own gender declaration where the child is able to give it. Birth sex registration remains male-or-female only and cannot be changed except to correct an initial error, but it ceases upon gender registration. The same laws let parents choose whether a child's gender is recorded, allow a person to remove a gender descriptor entirely, permit parents to change a child's legal gender, and extend the registration period for parents of intersex children to 120 days after birth. Tasmania issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates as of 2019.

The 2019 reforms passed the Tasmanian House of Assembly on 10 April 2019 after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition, the bill having already passed the Legislative Council. They made gender on birth certificates optional and removed the requirement that transgender people undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised. The Tasmanian Government opposed the amendments and declined to rule out later repeal; no repeal is recorded in the sources reviewed.

The age of consent in Tasmania is 17 years, equal for all forms of sexual activity, a figure shared only with South Australia.

A hate crimes bill passed the lower house in September 2025 and explicitly includes gender identity within the 1997 sentencing act. The upper house had not voted on it in the sources reviewed.

Cross-dressing was an offence under section 8(1)(d) of the Police Offences Act 1935 until its repeal on 12 April 2001, Tasmania having been the only Australian state to criminalise it. Charges and convictions under that provision as in force before 12 April 2001, including attempts and inciting, instigating, aiding or abetting, are eligible for expungement on application under the Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017, which received royal assent on 21 November 2017, with expungement available from 9 April 2018 and compensation of up to $75,000 available from 2 August 2026. The expungement scheme followed a parliamentary apology on 13 April 2017.

As of September 2026 conversion therapy practices remain legally permitted within Tasmania.

Same-sex couples can enter registered domestic partnerships in Tasmania with an optional official ceremony.

No state-specific incident series, enforcement pattern or trans-specific violence figure for Tasmania appears in the sources reviewed.
tangentialFactors:
The equal-status position on gender recognition was secured against government resistance rather than against any criminalisation or incident series: the Tasmanian Government opposed the 2019 birth-certificate amendments and did not rule out repeal, and the bill passed only after the lower-house speaker crossed the floor.

Tasmania's historical legal regime was among the harshest in the region. Consensual homosexual activity was decriminalised by the Criminal Code Amendment Act 1997, passed 1 May 1997 with assent 13 May 1997 and effect the following day, after penalties of up to 21 years, and Tasmania was the final Australian jurisdiction to decriminalise, doing so with effect from 14 May 1997 after the Commonwealth Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994 and in the face of a likely High Court loss in Croome v Tasmania. Cross-dressing remained an offence until 2001.

Equality of adoption rights for same-sex couples applied in all states and territories of Australia from April 2018, and federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto relationships since 2009; those layers sit above Tasmania's own registered-partnership scheme.

The two pending items in this record are both legislative: the hate crimes bill's upper-house vote, and the unexercised possibility of repeal flagged by the Tasmanian Government in 2019.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change for a Tasmanian-registered birth requires only a statutory declaration of identity and lived or seeking-to-live gender. There is no forced divorce, no sex reassignment surgery and no other medical requirement, and the Registrar holds a refusal power limited to terms outside those prescribed.

People aged 16 and over change their registered gender without parental permission. For under-16s the parent or guardian registers, using the child's own declaration where the child can give it, otherwise statements of consistency with the child's will and preference, with optional counselling evidence where the person is under 18.

Historic cross-dressing convictions are expungable on application to the Secretary by the person charged or, where that person is deceased or lacks capacity, by specified representatives. Compensation of up to $75,000 became available on 2 August 2026.

Registered domestic partnerships are available to same-sex couples with an optional official ceremony.

Conversion therapy practices remain legally permitted as of September 2026, so no statutory restriction protects a resident from them.

Discrimination on gender identity, gender expression, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics is prohibited by the Anti-Discrimination Act 1998, and the Act also reaches conduct that offends, humiliates, intimidates, insults or ridicules on those bases.
outOfScopeNotes:
The upper-house vote on the September 2025 hate crimes bill is not sourced, so whether gender identity now sits within the 1997 sentencing act remains unresolved in this record.

No charging, prosecution or complaint data for the Anti-Discrimination Act 1998, including its incitement-of-hatred provision, appears in the sources reviewed; enforcement practice is unresolved.

No trans-specific violence, homicide or victimisation figure for Tasmania is sourced, and no incident series is documented. The absence of such data is not evidence of absence.

Whether the Tasmanian Government pursued the repeal it declined to rule out in 2019 is not sourced.

Processing times, refusal practice and fee levels under the gender-registration declaration process are not sourced, nor is uptake of the expungement or compensation schemes.

The status of any move to restrict conversion therapy in Tasmania after September 2026 is not sourced.
